roman: hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ aisī ki har ḳhvāhish pe dam nikle
bahut nikle mire armān lekin phir bhī kam nikle
nuance_note: 'nikle' works three ways: 'dam nikalna' (breath leaving, i.e. dying for each desire), 'armān nikalna' (desires fulfilled) and 'kam nikalna' (turned out too few). The irony that even many fulfilled desires fall short must survive.

A.literal:
Thousands of desires such that for every desire, life departs,
Many of my longings were fulfilled, but still, they were few.
A.poetic:
Thousands of desires, each enough to steal the breath away,
Many longings were sated, yet far too few to stay.
notes: The core of the couplet is a brilliant pun on the verb 'nikalna' (to exit/emerge).
In the first line, 'dam nikle' is an idiom meaning to die or to be breathless with intensity/pain.
In the second line, 'armān nikle' is an idiom meaning that a longing was fulfilled (literally, the desire 'came out' into reality).
Ghalib creates a paradox: the desires are so powerful they are lethal, yet the fulfillment of those desires is insufficient to satisfy the soul.

B.literal:
Thousands of desires are such that at each desire the breath would depart.
Many of my longings came out, but still they came out few.
B.poetic:
Thousands of desires, each one worth the dying breath—
Many of my longings came to pass, yet still they were too few.
notes: dam nikalnā is an idiom for dying; literally it means 'breath coming out'. The literal keeps the breath image, while the poetic 'worth the dying breath' captures the idiomatic force.

The verb nikalnā is used twice: first with dam (breath departs/die) and then with armān (longings emerge/are fulfilled). English cannot use one verb for both senses; the literal uses 'came out' for both, while the poetic shifts to 'came to pass' for the second.

armān means heart's longings or desires, often with a sense of unfulfilled yearning. The second line's paradox—many came out, yet still few—suggests infinite desire: even many fulfilled longings feel insufficient.
The first line is hyperbolic: thousands of desires, each intense enough that one could die at/for it. It sets up the second line's many/few paradox.
This couplet does not contain Ghalib's takhallus, so no pen-name handling is needed.

C.literal:
Thousands of desires, such that on every desire the breath departs
Many of my longings were fulfilled, but even then they were few
C.poetic:
A thousand desires, each so intense they steal my breath,
Many longings were realized, yet they still feel far too few.
notes: The idiom 'dam nikle' (breath departs) is a double entendre: it refers to the physical sensation of being breathless from passion and the literal metaphor for dying from the agony of unfulfilled longing.
Ghalib employs a subtle shift in vocabulary from 'ḳhvāhish' (desire) in the first line to 'armān' (longing/aspiration) in the second to avoid repetition while deepening the emotional texture.

The verb 'nikle' (to emerge/to depart/to be fulfilled) acts as a pivot: in the first line, it describes the departure of life (death), whereas in the second, it describes the 'coming out' or fulfillment of wishes.
The couplet explores the existential paradox of human desire: the more one fulfills, the more one realizes the infinite nature of what remains unfulfilled.

roman: na thā kuchh to ḳhudā thā kuchh na hotā to ḳhudā hotā
Duboyā mujh ko hone ne na hotā maiñ to kyā hotā
nuance_note: Built on 'honā' (to be). Before anything was, God was; had nothing been, God would be; my being drowned me. Had I not been, what would I have been? Implies merging into God (waḥdat al-wujūd). Keep the repetition of 'being'.

A.literal:
When nothing was, God was; had nothing been, God would have been.
My existence has drowned me; had I not been, what would I have been?
A.poetic:
When nothing existed, God was; had nothing been, God would still be.
My very being has undone me; had I not been, what would I have been?
notes: The repetition of 'hota' (was/would be) creates a rhythmic, circular logic that mirrors the eternal nature of the Divine versus the transient nature of creation.
The word 'Duboyā' (drowned) is a classic Sufi metaphor: the 'ego' or the 'self' (the state of 'being') is what drowns the soul in the illusion of separation from the Divine Unity (Wahdat al-Wujud).
The poem presents a profound ontological paradox: the poet's existence is both his reality and his ruin, as 'being' is the very thing that creates the barrier between the lover and the Beloved.
The final question 'what would I have been?' is a rhetorical play on the impossibility of the self existing outside the context of its own struggle with existence.

B.literal:
When nothing was, God was; had nothing been, God would be.
My existence has drowned me; had I not been, what would I have been?
B.poetic:
When nothing existed, God was; had nothing been, God would remain.
My very being has undone me; had I not been, what might I have been?
notes: The couplet explores 'Wahdat-al-Wujūd' (Unity of Existence), the Sufi concept that only one True Reality exists.
The word 'duboyā' (drowned) is a double entendre: it refers to both worldly ruin and the spiritual tragedy of the soul being 'submerged' in the illusion of a separate identity (the ego).
The phrase 'hone ne' (the act of being) treats existence as an event or a catalyst for downfall, rather than a gift.

The final question 'kyā hotā' is a rhetorical paradox. While it asks 'what would I be?', the implied answer is 'I would have been God' or 'I would have remained in the Divine essence,' since the first line establishes that in the absence of 'something,' only God exists.

C.literal:
When nothing was, God was; if nothing were, God would be.
Being drowned me; if I were not, then what would be?
C.poetic:
When nothing was, God was; if nothing were, God would be.
Being has drowned me; had I not been, what would there be?
notes: The first line uses a conditional/correlative structure to assert God's necessary existence independent of all contingent things.
The repeated forms of honā (thā, hotā, hotā, hone, hotā, hotā) create a dense philosophical wordplay on being, existence, and non-existence.
Duboyā literally means 'drowned'; I keep the water image in the poetic version because it is vivid, though idiomatically it means 'ruined/undid me.'
Hone ne personifies being/existence as the agent that drowns the speaker—existence itself is the calamity.
The final kyā hotā is deliberately ambiguous: it can mean 'what would exist?', 'what would happen?', or 'what would it matter?' I chose 'what would there be?' to keep the existential question open.
The sher has no pen-name (takhallus) in this couplet, so none is rendered.

roman: dil-e-nādāñ tujhe huā kyā hai
āḳhir is dard kī davā kyā hai
nuance_note: Simple address to the naive heart: what has happened to you, what cure is there for this pain? Checks that the model doesn't over-embellish plain diction.

A.literal:
O naive heart, what has happened to you?
After all, what is the cure for this pain?
A.poetic:
O foolish heart, what has come over you?
What is the remedy, at last, for this pain?
notes: The poet employs the trope of addressing the heart as a separate, sentient, and stubborn entity (dil-e-nādāñ), a common feature in the ghazal tradition to express internal conflict.

The word 'dard' (pain) refers specifically to the 'pain of love' (ishq), which in Sufi and classical poetry is often viewed as a transformative or even desirable state rather than something to be simply eliminated.
The word 'āḳhir' suggests a sense of desperation or a final, exhausted inquiry, moving from a question of 'what' to a question of 'how to fix it'.

B.literal:
O naive heart, what has happened to you?
After all, what is the remedy for this pain?
B.poetic:
O foolish heart, what ails thee?
At last, what cure for this agony?
notes: The term 'dil-e-nādāñ' (naive heart) is a classic trope in the ghazal where the poet personifies the heart as a separate, somewhat incompetent entity that has foolishly surrendered to passion.
The repetition of the question 'kyā hai' (what is) creates a sense of circularity and existential helplessness, a hallmark of Ghalib's style.
The 'dard' (pain) is not merely physical but refers to the 'malady of love,' which in Sufi metaphysics is the necessary suffering required to strip away the ego.
The 'davā' (remedy) creates a structural tension; in the logic of the ghazal, the cure for the pain of love is often the very thing that causes it (the Beloved).

C.literal: O naive heart, what has happened to you? / After all, what is the cure for this pain?
C.poetic: O foolish heart, what has come over you? / In the end, what is the remedy for this pain?
notes: dil-e-nādāñ is an apostrophe to the heart; nādāñ can mean naive, innocent, or foolish. I use 'naive heart' in the literal version and 'foolish heart' in the poetic version to keep the affectionate reproach.
āḳhir carries both 'at last' and 'after all,' implying a long, fruitless search for a cure. I render it as 'After all' literally and 'In the end' poetically to preserve that double edge.
dard/davā (pain/remedy) is a stock ghazal pairing. The pain is left unnamed, so it can suggest worldly love, existential longing, or Sufi divine longing.
The second line is a rhetorical question with no answer, a common ghazal gesture of helplessness.
No takhallus (pen name) appears in this sher.

roman: ishq ne 'ġhālib' nikammā kar diyā
varna ham bhī aadmī the kaam ke
nuance_note: Contrast of 'nikammā' (useless) with 'aadmī the kaam ke' (a man of use). Self-mocking tone, pen name in the final couplet.

A.literal:
Love has rendered Ghalib useless,
otherwise I too was a man of use.
A.poetic:
Love has made Ghalib a wasted shell,
else I too was a man of merit.
notes: The core of the couplet is the wordplay between 'nikammā' (useless/without work) and 'kaam ke' (useful/of work), creating a sharp contrast between the poet's current state and his former potential.
The use of the pen name 'Ghalib' (meaning 'Dominant' or 'Overpowering') is deeply ironic here; the one whose name signifies dominance has been completely subdued and rendered powerless by love.
The pronoun 'ham' (we) is the royal plural often used by Ghalib to maintain a sense of persona and dignity even while admitting failure.

B.literal:
Love has made Ghalib useless,
Otherwise, I too was a man of use.
B.poetic:
Love has rendered Ghalib quite idle,
Else, I too was a man of worth.
notes: The Takhallus (pen name): Ghalib uses his own name, which means 'the conqueror' or 'the dominant one,' to create a sharp irony: the man whose name implies mastery has been completely defeated and rendered 'useless' by love.
The Dichotomy: The couplet hinges on the linguistic opposition between 'nikammā' (socially useless/idle) and 'kaam ke' (capable/productive).

The Lover's Paradox: In the ghazal tradition, the lover is often viewed by society as a madman or a wastrel. Ghalib adopts this self-deprecating persona, playing with the idea that his preoccupation with the Beloved has stripped him of his worldly competence.
Humor and Wit: Unlike the heavy, tragic tone of many Sufi poets, Ghalib employs a conversational, almost nonchalant wit (zarafat) to discuss his own spiritual or emotional undoing.
The Royal 'We': The use of 'ham' (we) is the standard poetic convention for the first-person singular, providing a sense of dignity even while discussing his 'uselessness'.

C.literal:
Love made Ghalib useless;
otherwise I too was a man of work.
C.poetic:
Love has rendered Ghalib good-for-nothing—
otherwise I too was a man of use.
notes: The pen name 'Ghalib' means 'dominant' or 'victor,' so there is irony in the one named dominant being made useless by love.
'Kaam ke aadmi' is an idiom for a useful, capable person; I rendered it as 'man of use/useful man.'
The register is deliberately colloquial ('nikamma,' 'kaam ke'), giving the couplet a wry, self-deprecating humor.
The first-person 'hum' is a conventional poetic/royal plural; English uses 'I'.
In the ghazal tradition, love's ruin of worldly competence can carry Sufi overtones of self-annihilation, though here the tone is more witty than mystical.

roman: ham ko ma.alūm hai jannat kī haqīqat lekin
dil ke ḳhush rakhne ko 'ġhālib' ye ḳhayāl achchhā hai
nuance_note: Sceptical irony: I know the truth about paradise, but it is a nice thought to keep the heart happy. Must not become pious or flatly atheist.

A.literal:
We know the reality of paradise, but
To keep the heart happy, Ghalib, this thought is good.
A.poetic:
The truth of Paradise is known to us, it's true,
But to soothe the heart, Ghalib, this fancy will do.
notes: The central tension lies in the juxtaposition of 'haqīqat' (reality/truth) and 'khayāl' (thought/fancy/delusion), contrasting the cold intellect with the emotional needs of the heart.
The reference to 'jannat' (paradise) carries a typical Ghalibian irony; he suggests that the promised afterlife is a simplistic construct or a 'useful fiction' rather than a spiritual destination.
The use of the takhallus (pen name) 'Ghalib' acts as a self-address, creating a sense of detached observation where the poet speaks to himself about his own self-deception.

B.literal:
We know the reality of Paradise, but
for keeping the heart happy, Ghalib, this idea is good.
B.poetic:
We know the truth of Paradise, but still,
to keep the heart glad, Ghalib, this fancy is good.
notes: The central contrast is between haqīqat (reality/truth) and khayāl (thought/fancy/illusion). Ghalib claims knowledge of Paradise's true nature but values the comforting thought over that knowledge.
dil ke khush rakhne ko is an idiom meaning to console oneself or keep one's spirits up; I rendered it as 'to keep the heart glad/content.'
Ghalib is the poet's pen name (takhallus) in the final-line self-address, a standard ghazal convention. The name means 'victor/dominant,' though that meaning is not especially active here.
jannat carries Islamic and Quranic associations of Paradise; English 'Paradise' keeps some of that weight but not the everyday religious familiarity.

C.literal:
We know the reality of paradise, but
To keep the heart happy, Ghalib, this thought is good
C.poetic:
We know the truth of paradise, and yet
To soothe the heart, Ghalib, this fancy is quite fine
notes: The core of the sher lies in the dialectic between 'haqīqat' (objective reality/truth) and 'ḳhayāl' (subjective thought/imagination/notion).
Ghalib employs a signature philosophical skepticism, suggesting that the religious promise of paradise might be a psychological coping mechanism—a 'pleasant thought'—rather than an ontological fact.
The phrase 'dil ke khush rakhne ko' functions as an idiom for providing a comforting delusion or an appeasement of human desire.
The use of the first-person plural 'ham' (we) shifts the tone from a personal doubt to a universal, almost detached, observation of the human condition.
The takhallus (pen name) 'Ghalib' is used here to add a layer of self-aware wit, as if the poet is commenting on his own cynical or clever observation.

roman: naqsh fariyādī hai kis kī shoḳhi-e-tahrīr kā
kāġhzī hai pairahan har paikar-e-tasvīr kā
nuance_note: Famously opaque opening of the Diwan. Alludes to the Persian custom of petitioners wearing paper robes before a ruler: every figure in the picture wears paper, complaining against the playful pen of its maker. Needs annotation; a bare literal version is meaningless.

A.literal: The image complains of whose playfulness of writing? / Paper is the garment of every figure of the picture.
A.poetic: A painted figure cries out—against whose playful pen? / Each image wears a paper robe, again and again.
notes: naqsh means both a painted/drawn figure and a written character or trace, so the line conflates picture and writing.
fariyādī is a legal complainant/plaintiff: the image is not merely sad but formally lodging a grievance against the artist's caprice.
shoḳhī-e-tahrīr means the playful wit or mischief of the pen/script, suggesting both dazzling calligraphic style and arbitrary creative power.
kāġhzī pairahan is both literal—the only garment of a painted figure is the paper surface—and symbolic—its body/clothing is insubstantial, fragile, paper-thin.
In a Sufi register, all phenomenal forms are figures in a divine artwork, wearing paper-thin robes, complaining of the painter’s will.

B.literal:
The image is a complainant of whose playful writing?
Every figure of the picture has a garment of paper.
B.poetic:
The image pleads: whose mischievous hand drew me so?
For every form in this portrait wears a shroud of paper.
notes: Tahrir: Ghalib uses 'writing' to refer to the act of painting/drawing, blurring the line between the calligrapher and the artist.
Fariyadi: This is a legal term for a plaintiff. The image is not just sad, but is formally lodging a complaint against its creator for the limitation of its existence.
Shokhi: This word captures a blend of brilliance, playfulness, and a certain cruel irony. The artist's 'play' is the subject's 'prison'.
Kaghzi pairahan: A masterful metaphor. The 'clothing' of the figure is the very paper it is drawn on. This suggests that the figure's entire being is fragile, two-dimensional, and artificial.

C.literal:
The image is a complainant against whose playful writing?
The garment of every figure in the picture is made of paper.
C.poetic:
The sketch cries out: 'Whose playful stroke is this?'
For every form in the painting wears a garment of paper.
notes: Shoḳhi-e-tahrīr: This refers to the 'mischievous' or 'vivacious' stroke of the pen or brush. In a Sufi context, it alludes to the capricious or playful nature of the Divine Creator's hand in fashioning the universe.

The Paradox of Existence: The 'naqsh' (the created image) is a 'fariyādī' (complainant) because it realizes its own ontological fragility. It complains against the very 'writing' (the act of creation) that brought it into being, because that creation reveals its substance to be nothing but paper.

Metaphor of Paper: Ghalib uses 'paper' to symbolize the ephemeral, thin, and unsubstantial nature of physical existence. The 'garment' (outer appearance) and the 'form' (the body) are both equally fragile.

Naqsh vs. Tasvīr: There is a subtle distinction between 'naqsh' (the mark, the sketch, or the imprint) and 'tasvīr' (the completed visual representation), emphasizing the process of being 'written' into existence.

roman: koī ummīd bar nahīñ aatī
koī sūrat nazar nahīñ aatī
nuance_note: 'bar aana' = to be fulfilled. 'sūrat' = face and also way out or form: no face appears / no way appears. Flag the double sense.

A.literal:
No hope comes to fruition,
No way/face appears to the eye.
A.poetic:
No hope ever comes to fruition,
No way out, no face, in my vision.
notes: 'Bar āna' is a Persian idiom meaning for a hope or wish to be realized or to materialize.

'Sūrat' is a polysemous word: it means the 'face' of the beloved, but also a 'way,' 'method,' or 'solution' to a problem. Ghalib uses this to conflate the longing for the beloved with the longing for an end to his misery.
The repetition of 'koī... nahīñ aatī' (the radif) creates a rhythmic sense of stagnation and absolute despair, mirroring the poet's feeling of being trapped.

B.literal:
No hope comes upon [me]
No face/form is visible
B.poetic:
No hope comes to my aid,
No face appears to my gaze.
notes: Sūrat: This is the central pun of the couplet. In the ghazal tradition, it refers to the 'face' or 'form' of the beloved (the object of desire), but it also carries the meaning of a 'way out' or a 'solution' (as in the phrase 'sūrat-e-haal'). The poet is expressing a dual despair: he cannot see the beloved, and he cannot see a way to resolve his suffering.

Ummīd: While literally 'hope,' in a Sufi context, hope can be seen as a lingering attachment to the possibility of worldly or even spiritual union, which prevents total annihilation (fana). Its absence signifies a state of absolute, hollow desolation.
Bar: Used here to complete the meter, it implies that no hope is 'arriving' or 'manifesting' to the poet's current state.

C.literal:
No hope comes to fulfillment;
No face/form/way appears to sight.
C.poetic:
No hope bears fruit,
No face appears to view.
notes: The idiom bar ānā means to come to pass, succeed, or be fulfilled; I render it as 'bears fruit' to keep the sense of fruition.
sūrat carries multiple meanings: face, countenance, form, appearance, and also way or means. The line can suggest both the beloved's absence and the lack of any solution.
The repeated koī with negatives gives an absolute sweep: not a single hope, not a single face or way.
nazar ānā means 'to become visible,' so the speaker is not merely failing to see; nothing presents itself to sight.

roman: reḳhte ke tumhīñ ustād nahīñ ho 'ġhālib'
kahte haiñ agle zamāne meñ koī 'mīr' bhī thā
nuance_note: 'Rekhta' is the old name for Urdu poetry; 'Mīr' is Mir Taqi Mir. Ghalib names himself and concedes an earlier master. Both names and the literary-history context need explaining.

A.literal:
You are not the [only] master of Rekhte, Ghalib,
They say that in the previous era, there was also a Mir.
A.poetic:
You are not the sole master of this art, Ghalib,
They say in days gone by, there lived a Mir as well.
notes: The poet uses 'Rekhte' to refer to the Urdu language, emphasizing its nature as a hybrid of Persian and local dialects.

There is a sophisticated play on the pen names: 'Ghalib' means 'dominant' or 'victorious', while 'Mir' means 'chief' or 'leader'. By acknowledging Mir, Ghalib ironically challenges his own 'dominance'.

The tone is one of 'shaguftagi' (playfulness/wit). Ghalib is not genuinely humble; he is engaging in a literary dialogue with his predecessor, Mir Taqi Mir, acknowledging him to elevate the conversation.
The phrase 'agle zamāne' literally means 'the next time' but idiomatically refers to the 'previous era' in this context.

B.literal:
You are not the master of Rekhta, O Ghalib,
They say in the previous era, there was also a Mir.
B.poetic:
You are no master of Rekhta, Ghalib, they say,
For in an earlier age, a Mir held sway.
notes: Rekhta refers to the classical form of the Urdu language, emphasizing the poet's command over its specific linguistic texture.
Mir is a profound allusion to Mir Taqi Mir, the undisputed 'God of Poetry' (Khuda-e-Sukhan) and the greatest master of the Urdu ghazal.
The couplet employs 'tazmeen' or a conversational irony where Ghalib adopts a self-deprecating tone to pay homage to his predecessor.
The wordplay lies in the juxtaposition of the two giants: by acknowledging Mir's supremacy, Ghalib subtly places himself in the same breath as the greatest, creating a dialogue across time.
Ghalib's pen name, 'Ghalib' (meaning dominant/overpowering), creates a subtle tension with the humble claim that he is not the master.

C.literal:
Of Rekhta, you alone are not the master, Ghalib—
They say in the earlier age there was also someone called Mir.
C.poetic:
You are not the only master of Rekhta, Ghalib—
They say in times gone by there was also one Mir.
notes: Rekhta is the older term for Urdu poetry, specifically the mixed Persian-Urdu poetic idiom; using it signals the classical tradition Ghalib is being measured against.
The pen name 'Ghalib' means 'dominant' or 'victor' — the couplet ironically undercuts the boast implicit in the name by reminding him of a predecessor.
Mir Taqi Mir (1723–1810) was the great Urdu ghazal poet of the previous generation, often called 'Khuda-e Sukhan' (God of Poetry). Ghalib himself acknowledged Mir's greatness.
The word 'mīr' also means 'leader' or 'chief', so the line works doubly: there was a poet named Mir, and there was a 'chief' of poetry before you.
The address to himself in the third person using his pen name is a standard ghazal convention (takhallus), here used for self-irony rather than self-praise.
The tone is wry and self-deprecating on the surface, but it also asserts Ghalib's own standing by placing him in direct comparison with Mir — only a true master could be addressed this way.

roman: bas-ki dushvār hai har kaam kā āsāñ honā
aadmī ko bhī mayassar nahīñ insāñ honā
nuance_note: 'aadmī' (a human being) vs 'insāñ' (a humane person): even a man can't easily be human. English 'man/human' tends to collapse the distinction. 'bas-ki' is archaic for 'so much so'.

A.literal:
So difficult it is for every task to be easy,
Even for a man, it is not attainable to be human.
A.poetic:
So arduous is the art of making every burden light,
That even man finds it hard to reach the height of humanity.
notes: The crux of the couplet lies in the distinction between 'aadmī' and 'insāñ'. While both translate to 'human' or 'man' in English, Ghalib uses 'aadmī' to denote the biological species (the physical being) and 'insāñ' to denote the ideal of humanity (the moral, spiritual, and ethical perfection).

The first line establishes a philosophical paradox: the 'difficulty of ease.' This sets the stage for the second line, suggesting that the most difficult 'task' of all is the transition from being a biological human to a virtuous one.
The word 'mayassar' implies not just availability, but something granted or made possible, often suggesting a divine or circumstantial allowance.

B.literal:
Because it is difficult for every task to be easy,
Even for a man, it is not possible to be a human.
B.poetic:
Since ease is a rarity for every endeavor,
Even a man finds it hard to be truly human.
notes: The crux of the couplet is the semantic distinction between 'aadmī' and 'insāñ'. In Urdu/Persian thought, 'aadmī' refers to the biological species (man), while 'insāñ' refers to the perfected human being who possesses true empathy, morality, and spiritual awareness.
Ghalib employs a logical syllogism: if the simplest tasks in life are inherently difficult, then the most profound task—the attainment of true humanity—must be nearly impossible.
The word 'mayassar' carries a sense of being 'granted' or 'made available,' suggesting that true humanity is not just a matter of effort, but a state of grace or a rare existential achievement.

C.literal:
So difficult is the becoming easy of every task
Even for man, becoming human is not attainable
C.poetic:
So hard is it for any task to become easy—
even a man cannot attain to being truly human.
notes: The central wordplay is aadmī versus insāñ: both can mean 'man/human,' but aadmī suggests the ordinary biological or social human (literally 'son of Adam'), while insāñ carries moral and Sufi overtones of true, perfected humanity.
The first line's paradox—difficulty of ease—sets up the second line's paradox: a human failing to become truly human.
bas-ki works as an intensifier meaning 'to such an extent that,' making the second line a consequence of the first.
mayassar implies something granted or made available, not merely possible by effort, which suits the spiritual register.
The verbal noun honā can mean 'being' or 'becoming'; I use 'becoming' to emphasize the movement from aadmī to insāñ.

roman: un ke dekhe se jo aa jaatī hai muñh par raunaq
vo samajhte haiñ ki bīmār kā haal achchhā hai
nuance_note: Seeing the beloved brings colour to the lover's face, so she thinks the sick man is well. Keep the bittersweet misreading.

A.literal:
Because of seeing them, a glow appears on the face;
They assume that the condition of the sick person is good.
A.poetic:
The glow that lights my face the moment they appear,
Makes them believe the sick man's recovery is near.
notes: The 'bimaar' (sick person) is a stock symbol in the ghazal tradition representing the lover, whose 'illness' is the longing and agony caused by love.

The irony lies in the misinterpretation: the beloved sees the momentary flush of joy (raunaq) caused by their presence and mistakes it for a sign of health, unaware that they are the very cause of the lover's sickness.
The use of 'un' (plural/respectful) maintains the distance and dignity of the beloved, a common trope in Ghalib's poetry.

B.literal:
From their seeing, the glow that comes over the face —
they think that the sick one's condition is good.
B.poetic:
The colour that their looking brings into my face
they take for the sick man's improving state.
notes: raunaq means lustre, bloom, or radiance; in the ghazal world the beloved's presence gives the lover's face a false, excited colour.
The irony is that the beloved reads the lover's flush as recovery, though it is caused only by the beloved's visit—presence, not cure.
un ke dekhe se can mean 'from their seeing him' or 'from his seeing them'; the translation has to choose one while the Urdu holds both.
bimar is the stock love-sick lover; his illness is longing, and looking healthy may make the beloved feel free to leave.

C.literal:
The radiance that comes upon the face from their sight,
They think that the patient's condition is good.
C.poetic:
The glow that graces my face at the sight of them,
Leads them to believe the sufferer is well.
notes: The word 'raunaq' (radiance/bloom) is a crucial double entendre: it refers to the spiritual/emotional glow of seeing the Beloved, but also to the physical flush of a feverish face.
The 'bīmār' (sick person) is a classical trope in the ghazal, representing the lover whose 'ailment' is the madness of love.
The irony of the couplet lies in the misinterpretation: the very symptom of the lover's intense, feverish passion is mistaken by the Beloved for a sign of physical health and recovery.
The use of 'un' (them/their) is the formal/honorific plural used to refer to the Beloved, maintaining a sense of distance and reverence.

roman: bāzīcha-e-atfāl hai duniyā mire aage
hotā hai shab-o-roz tamāshā mire aage
nuance_note: 'bāzīcha-e-atfāl' = a children's playground. The world is a spectacle staged before me night and day. Tone: detached and lofty, not dismissive.

A.literal:
The world is a children's playground before me
Night and day a spectacle keeps happening before me
A.poetic:
The world before me is a child's plaything,
A spectacle unceasing spread before me.
notes: bāzīcha-e-atfāl literally means 'plaything of children' — the earth as a toy or game that children play with, implying its impermanence and triviality from the speaker's elevated perspective.

mire aage has a double sense: spatial (before my eyes) and temporal (ahead of my life / still to come), and can also carry the Sufi connotation of 'in the presence of my true self or God-consciousness'.

tamāshā is a key Mughal-era word: it means spectacle, entertainment, show — often used for public performances or curiosities. Here it suggests the world's affairs are a passing show watched with detachment.
shab-o-roz (night and day) is an idiom for 'constantly / ceaselessly'.
The repeated 'mire aage' at the end of both lines works as a refrain-like stress, which I kept by ending both English lines with 'before me'.
Ghalib is not using his pen name (takhallus) in this two-line selection; it is not the closing couplet of the ghazal.

B.literal:
The world is a children's playground before me,
A spectacle takes place night and day before me.
B.poetic:
The world is but a child's plaything in my sight,
A ceaseless pageant, day and night, in my sight.
notes: The phrase 'bāzīcha-e-atfāl' reduces the complexities of human existence, politics, and suffering to a trivial game, reflecting a state of detached cynicism or Sufi transcendence.

The word 'tamāshā' carries a double meaning: it can be a wondrous spectacle or a ridiculous farce. Given Ghalib's typical irony, it suggests the world is a theatrical performance of no real consequence.
The repetition of 'mire aage' (before me) acts as the radif, centering the poet as the sole, detached observer of this cosmic play.

C.literal:
The world is a children's playground before me
A spectacle happens night and day before me
C.poetic:
The world is but a children's game before my eyes,
A ceaseless spectacle unfolds, night and day, before me.
notes: bāzīcha-e-atfāl: A Persian construction used here to diminish the gravity of existence, suggesting the world lacks true substance or consequence.
tamāshā: This term implies a theatrical performance or a passing amusement, reinforcing the idea that worldly events are merely an illusion or a fleeting show.

The Spectator Motif: The repetition of 'mire aage' (before me) establishes the poet's persona as a detached observer. This reflects a Sufi-inflected philosophical stance where the individual has transcended worldly attachments to view existence from a distance.
The duality of 'shab-o-roz' (night and day) emphasizes the relentless, cyclical, and ultimately futile nature of the worldly drama.

roman: haiñ aur bhī duniyā meñ suḳhan-var bahut achchhe
kahte haiñ ki 'ġhālib' kā hai andāz-e-bayāñ aur
nuance_note: The repeated end word 'aur' means 'other/different': Ghalib's style of expression is something else. A boast that works through that final word.

A.literal:
There are many other very good poets in the world
They say that Ghalib's style of expression is different
A.poetic:
Many other fine poets the world may hold,
Yet they say Ghalib's style is something more.
notes: The word 'aur' (more/other/different) serves as a semantic pivot. In the first line, it is a quantifier meaning 'other' or 'additional' poets; in the second line, it shifts to a qualitative descriptor meaning 'different' or 'extraordinary'.

The use of 'kahte haiñ' (they say) is a rhetorical device of 'indirect boasting.' By attributing the praise to 'them,' Ghalib maintains a veneer of poetic modesty while asserting his supreme uniqueness.
Andāz-e-bayāñ is a technical term in Urdu poetics referring to the distinct rhetorical voice or 'manner' that separates a master from a mere practitioner.
The couplet is a classic example of Ghalib's 'self-praise' (faqr), which is characterized by intellectual wit rather than mere vanity.

B.literal:
There are other poets in the world who are very good,
They say that Ghalib's style of expression is different.
B.poetic:
Many a master of the word graces this world with art,
Yet they say Ghalib's voice sets him apart.
notes: The entire couplet hinges on the word 'aur' (اور). In the first line, it functions as a quantifier meaning 'others' or 'more'. In the second line, it functions as a qualitative adjective meaning 'different', 'unique', or 'something else entirely'.
Ghalib employs a rhetorical device of 'false humility'; by attributing the praise to others ('they say'), he elevates his own status while appearing to merely report common opinion.
The term 'suḳhan-var' implies not just a poet, but a craftsman of language, emphasizing that Ghalib is comparing himself to the elite of the literary world.

C.literal:
There are also many other very good poets in the world;
they say that Ghalib's style of expression is different.
C.poetic:
The world holds many a fine poet besides —
but Ghalib's voice, they say, is of another kind.
notes: The pen name 'Ghalib' appears in the second line, as required by the ghazal convention of takhallus (poetic signature) in the maqta (final couplet).

The word 'aur' (other/different) is the entire punch of the couplet — it is deliberately understated. Ghalib does not say 'better', only 'different', but the implication of uniqueness and superiority is unmistakable. I rendered this as 'of another kind' to preserve the understated boast.
'Sukhan-var' literally means 'one who possesses speech/eloquence' — a stock term for poets in the classical tradition. I used 'poet' in the literal and 'fine poet' in the poetic version.

'Andāz-e-bayāñ' (style of expression) is a key aesthetic term in Urdu poetics, referring to a poet's distinctive manner or idiom. I kept 'style of expression' in the literal and shifted to 'voice' in the poetic rendering for naturalness.
The couplet is an ironic self-praise disguised as reported speech ('they say'), a common Ghalibian move — the modesty of the first line sets up the quiet boast of the second.

roman: ye masā.il-e-tasavvuf ye tirā bayān 'ġhālib'
tujhe ham valī samajhte jo na bāda-ḳhvār hotā
nuance_note: Mystical topics, such eloquence: we'd think you a saint (valī) if you weren't a wine-drinker. Leaves open whether the wine is literal or mystical; should not be resolved.

A.literal:
These problems of Sufism, this exposition of yours, Ghalib—
We would consider you a saint, if you were not a wine-drinker.
A.poetic:
These mysteries of the Sufi path, this discourse of yours, Ghalib—
We would have called you a saint, were you not a drinker of wine.
notes: masā.il-e-tasavvuf literally means 'questions/problems of Sufism,' suggesting intricate mystical doctrine.
bayān means exposition, statement, or style; here it praises Ghalib's eloquent speech.
valī is a Sufi saint or 'friend of God,' a high spiritual rank.
bāda-khvār literally means 'wine-drinker,' but in Sufi ghazal symbolism wine often stands for divine love or mystical intoxication, so the apparent disqualification is also a mystic credential.

The pen name Ghalib appears in the final-couplet self-address, and the wit lies in the mock condition: his speech sounds saintly, but his wine-drinking withholds sainthood—unless read through Sufi symbolism.

B.literal:
These complexities of Sufism, this discourse of yours, Ghalib,
We would have considered you a saint, if you were not a wine-drinker.
B.poetic:
Such Sufi depths, such eloquence in your speech, Ghalib,
We would have hailed you as a saint, were you not a drunkard.
notes: The poet uses his takhallus (pen name) 'Ghalib' to address himself, creating a dialogue between the speaker and the persona.

The tension lies in the contrast between 'tasavvuf' (spiritual mysticism) and 'bāda-ḳhvār' (drinking). In the Sufi tradition, wine is often a metaphor for divine love and spiritual intoxication, but it is also a literal vice in orthodox Islam.

The irony is that the poet's discourse is so profound that it mimics the wisdom of a 'wali' (saint), yet his outward habit of drinking disqualifies him from the formal title of sainthood in the eyes of the world.
The word 'masā.il' refers to legal or theological problems/points of discussion, suggesting that Ghalib is not just talking about love, but engaging in complex mystical theology.

C.literal:
These matters of Sufism, this discourse of yours, Ghalib,
We would have considered you a saint, if you were not a wine-drinker.
C.poetic:
These mystical questions, this way of yours, Ghalib—
We’d have deemed you a saint, had you not been a drinker of wine.
notes: Self-address: Ghalib uses his takhallus (pen name) to address himself, a common technique to create a dialogue between the poet's persona and his reputation.

The Paradox of the Saint and the Drunkard: The couplet plays on the tension between the 'faqir' (ascetic) and the 'bāda-khvār' (wine-drinker). In Sufi symbolism, wine often represents divine intoxication, but in the eyes of the orthodox, it is a vice that disqualifies one from sainthood.

Irony: There is a biting irony here; Ghalib suggests that his philosophical/mystical depth is so profound that it mimics the speech of a saint, yet his worldly reputation for drinking prevents him from being recognized as such.
Valī: This term implies more than just a 'holy man'; it refers to a high-ranking spiritual friend of God, making the contrast with his 'sinful' drinking even sharper.

roman: go haath ko jumbish nahīñ āñkhoñ meñ to dam hai
rahne do abhī sāġhar-o-mīnā mire aage
nuance_note: Hands can't move but the eyes still have life: leave the goblet and flask before me. Wine vessels as the poet's last attachment to life.

A.literal:
Although the hand has no movement, in the eyes there is still strength
Let the goblet and the flask remain before me still
A.poetic:
Though my hand cannot stir, my eyes yet hold their light
Leave the cup and the flask before me still
notes: The poet is likely depicting a state of terminal illness or extreme fragility, a common theme in Ghalib's later work.
The word 'dam' is a polysemy meaning breath, life, strength, or a moment. Here it signifies the vitality of the gaze.
The 'sāġhar' (cup) and 'mīnā' (flask) are stock symbols of the tavern (maikhana), representing both worldly intoxication and Sufi spiritual ecstasy.

The core paradox is the shift from physical consumption to visual consumption: the poet suggests that the mere sight of the wine is enough to sustain him or provide the desired intoxication, rendering the physical act of drinking unnecessary.

B.literal:
Although the hand has no movement, there is still breath in the eyes
Let the goblet and the flask remain before me
B.poetic:
Though my hand has lost its motion, my eyes still hold their breath;
Leave the goblet and the flask before me, just as they are.
notes: The contrast between 'jumbish' (physical agency/movement) and 'dam' (vitality/breath) highlights the threshold between life and death; the body is failing, but the soul's vision remains.
The 'eyes' having 'breath' is a poetic conceit suggesting that as long as the poet can behold his beloved or his symbols of ecstasy, he is truly alive.
'Sāġhar-o-mīnā' (the goblet and the flask) is a classic synecdoche for the tavern and the state of intoxication, representing the tools of spiritual or romantic ecstasy.

In the Sufi tradition, the wine and its vessels are symbols of Divine Love; the poet is requesting that his final moments be spent in a state of 'intoxication' (spiritual proximity) rather than the 'sobriety' of death.
The couplet captures the 'ghazal' ethos of clinging to one's identity and passion even in the face of inevitable physical dissolution.

C.literal: Though there is no movement in the hand, there is life in the eyes; / let the wine-cup and flagon remain before me for now.
C.poetic: Though the hand cannot stir, in the eyes there is still breath; / leave the cup and the wine-flask a while yet in front of me.
notes: 'dam' carries both 'breath/life' and 'moment,' so the eyes are still alive and still capable of a little while; English has to choose one sense.
The contrast between the motionless hand and the living eyes is an ironic image of weakness or age versus remaining desire.
'sāġhar-o-mīnā' are conventional wine implements; in the ghazal/Sufi register they can also suggest spiritual longing or divine wine, though the surface scene is literal.
'rahne do' is an imperative to a cup-bearer or attendant: do not remove the wine-things, since sight itself still sustains him.
The emphatic 'to' after 'āñkhoñ meñ' marks the eyes as the one thing still retaining life.

roman: aah ko chāhiye ik umr asar hote tak
kaun jiitā hai tirī zulf ke sar hote tak
nuance_note: A sigh needs a lifetime to take effect ('asar'); who lives long enough for your tresses to be won ('sar hona' = to be conquered, with 'sar' also meaning head/tip). Tresses (zulf) as the beloved's snare.

A.literal:
For a sigh, one lifetime is needed until effect happens.
Who lives until the end of your tress happens?
A.poetic:
A sigh needs a whole lifetime to take effect—
who lives until your tresses reach their end?
notes: The beloved’s zulf (long, curling, tangled tresses) is a stock ghazal image of endless beauty and entrapment; its tip or end (sar) is always receding.
The first line treats the lover’s aah as slow-acting: it only produces asar (effect) after a lifetime.
The original ends both lines with hote tak, creating a rhythmic echo, and plays on the sonic and visual closeness of asar (effect) and sar (tip/end/head).
kaun jiitā hai is a rhetorical question: ‘who lives long enough?’ implies no one can.
I rendered sar as ‘end/tip’ to preserve the impossible-distance image, but had to sacrifice its literal sense of ‘head’.

B.literal:
A sigh needs a lifetime until it has an effect
Who lives until your tresses are conquered?
B.poetic:
A sigh requires a lifetime to find its mark,
Who survives until your curls are finally undone?
notes: The 'aah' (sigh) is a stock symbol in the ghazal, representing the lover's spiritual and emotional suffering which is meant to eventually move the beloved or the Divine.
The 'zulf' (tresses) symbolizes the labyrinthine complexity of the beloved's beauty and the snares that trap the lover.
There is a sophisticated phonetic play (paronomasia) between 'asar' (effect) in the first line and 'sar' (head/conquer) in the second.
The phrase 'sar hona' is an idiom. In the context of 'zulf', it carries a double meaning: to unravel the knots of the curls, and to conquer or master the difficulty of the beloved's indifference.

C.literal:
A sigh requires a lifetime until it takes effect
Who lives until the ends of your tresses are reached?
C.poetic:
A sigh needs a lifetime to bear its effect,
Who lives to see your tresses reach their end?
notes: The rhyme (qafiya) links 'asar' (effect) with 'sar' (end/head), creating a structural parallel between the efficacy of a prayer/lament and the physical extent of the beloved's hair.
The 'sigh' (aah) is a classical symbol of the lover's spiritual and physical suffering, often used in Sufi poetry to represent the soul's longing for the Divine.
The 'tresses' (zulf) represent the beloved's beauty and the labyrinthine, winding complexity of the path of love.
The couplet employs a temporal irony: the lover's spiritual plea is too slow to be heard, and the beloved's physical beauty is too vast/endless to be fully witnessed before death.

The word 'sar' is used here to mean the 'end' or 'limit' of the hair, playing on the idea of the hair being so long or the process of its arrangement so slow that the lover cannot survive to see it completed.

roman: pattā pattā buuTā buuTā haal hamārā jaane hai
jaane na jaane gul hī na jaane baaġh to saarā jaane hai
nuance_note: Doubled words 'pattā pattā, buuTā buuTā' and the repeated 'jaane'. Every leaf knows my state; only the flower (the beloved) doesn't, though the whole garden does.

A.literal:
Leaf by leaf, plant by plant, knows our condition.
Whether it knows or not, even if the rose alone does not know, the whole garden indeed knows.
A.poetic:
Each leaf, each sprig, knows my plight.
The rose may not know—yet the whole garden knows.
notes: The doubled nouns pattā pattā and buuTā buuTā are an idiom of totality: every single leaf and plant, meaning all of nature or the whole world.
Gul (rose) is a stock ghazal symbol for the beloved, while bāġh (garden) can mean the surrounding world or society that witnesses the lover’s suffering.
The phrase jaane na jaane ... hī na jaane sets up a concessive contrast: even if the beloved/rose is ignorant or indifferent, the rest of creation is not.
I rendered hamārā as 'my' in the poetic version because the ghazal’s first-person plural often works as a formal or royal singular in English verse.

B.literal:
Every leaf, every bush knows my state,
Whether the flower knows or not, the entire garden knows.
B.poetic:
Every leaf, every bush knows my woe,
The garden knows all, though the flower does not know.
notes: The 'gul' (flower) is the standard ghazal symbol for the Beloved; the central irony is that the Beloved is the only part of the 'baaġh' (garden/world) that remains oblivious to the lover's 'haal' (state of suffering).

The repetition of 'pattā pattā' and 'buuTā buuTā' (leaf by leaf, bush by bush) serves to emphasize the overwhelming, all-encompassing nature of the lover's grief—it is a public spectacle rather than a private agony.

The couplet utilizes the trope of the 'indifferent beloved,' a common theme in Sufi poetry where the seeker's struggle is witnessed by the entire creation, yet the Divine/Beloved remains seemingly detached.

C.literal:
Every leaf, every shrub knows my condition,
Whether they know or not, only the flower knows not; the whole garden knows.
C.poetic:
Leaf by leaf, shrub by shrub, my plight is known to all,
All know it—save the Rose; the whole garden knows.
notes: The 'Gul' (Rose) is a stock symbol in the ghazal tradition representing the Beloved. The irony lies in the fact that the entire world (the garden) is a witness to the lover's suffering, yet the one person who is the cause of that suffering remains oblivious.
The repetition of 'pattā pattā buuTā buuTā' creates a rhythmic obsession, mirroring the lover's state of mind where every small detail of nature reflects his grief.
The phrase 'jaane na jaane' is a play on the word 'jaane' (to know). It functions as an idiomatic expression meaning 'whether they know or not,' while maintaining the sonic texture of the poem.

roman: nāzukī us ke lab kī kyā kahiye
pañkhuḌī ik gulāb kī sī hai
nuance_note: Simple, famous simile: the delicacy of her lip is like a rose petal. Tests restraint.

A.literal:
What can one say of the delicacy of those lips?
It is like a petal of a rose.
A.poetic:
How can one describe the delicacy of those lips?
They are like a single petal of a rose.
notes: The phrase 'kyā kahiye' is a rhetorical device used to express that the subject's beauty is so overwhelming that it transcends the capacity of language.
The rose (gulāb) is a stock symbol in the ghazal tradition for the ultimate standard of beauty and fragility.
The comparison is a 'tashbih' (simile), specifically focusing on the tactile quality of softness and the visual quality of a pale, tender hue.

B.literal:
The delicacy of those lips, what can be said?
They are like a petal of a rose.
B.poetic:
How can I describe the softness of those lips?
They are like a single rose petal.
notes: The concept of 'nazakat' (delicacy/finesse) is a central aesthetic in Urdu poetry, representing a beauty that is both physically soft and spiritually ethereal.
The phrase 'kyā kahiye' is a rhetorical trope used to signal that the subject's beauty is so profound that language fails to capture it.
The rose (gulāb) is the quintessential symbol of the beloved in the Persianate/Urdu tradition, representing perfection and transient beauty.

This couplet is a prime example of 'Sahl-e-Mumtana'—a style of poetry that appears deceptively simple and easy to compose, but is actually impossible to replicate due to its perfect balance and depth.

C.literal:
The delicacy of her lips—what can one say?
It is like a petal of a rose.
C.poetic:
What can one say of her lips' delicacy?
It is like a petal of a rose.
notes: The first line uses the idiomatic rhetorical question 'kyā kahiye' to claim that the lips' delicacy is beyond description.
The second line answers with a conventional ghazal simile: the beloved's lips are like a rose petal, evoking softness, fragility, and perhaps color.
nāzukī can mean delicacy, fineness, or fragility; I render it as 'delicacy' to keep the tactile and aesthetic sense.
The 'ik' before 'gulāb' can be read as 'a single' rose petal, subtly intensifying the image of fragility.
There is no significant wordplay or pen-name in this couplet; the effect lies in the rhetorical question and the stock simile.

roman: ulTī ho ga.iiñ sab tadbīreñ kuchh na davā ne kaam kiyā
dekhā is bīmāri-e-dil ne āḳhir kaam tamām kiyā
nuance_note: 'kaam kiyā' (medicine did not work) answered by 'kaam tamām kiyā' (finished me off). The pun on 'kaam' carries the couplet.

A.literal:
All my measures turned upside down, the medicine did no work;
I saw that this sickness of the heart finally finished the task.
A.poetic:
All my remedies failed, the medicine proved no avail;
I saw this heartache, at last, complete its fatal tale.
notes: The verse hinges on a sophisticated wordplay (paronomasia) involving the word 'kaam'.
In the first line, 'kaam kiyā' means to be effective or to function; the poet laments that the medicine failed to 'work'.
In the second line, 'kaam tamām kiyā' is a Persian-influenced Urdu idiom meaning 'to finish', 'to destroy', or 'to bring to an end'.
The irony is central: while the medicine failed to perform its 'work' (healing), the disease succeeded in its 'work' (killing).

The 'sickness of the heart' (bīmāri-e-dil) is a classical trope for the overwhelming passion of love, which in the Sufi tradition can also represent the soul's agonizing longing for the Divine that eventually consumes the ego.

B.literal:
All the plans were turned upside down; the medicine did no work.
I saw: this sickness of the heart at last did the work completely.
B.poetic:
All plans went awry; the remedy had no effect.
Behold, this heart-disease at last finished the job for good.
notes: The first line sets up medical and practical failure: tadbīr (plan/remedy) and davā (medicine) both fail, leaving no cure.
bīmāri-e-dil means both a physical heart disease and the traditional ghazal illness of love and longing; I keep ‘heart-disease’ to preserve both.
kaam tamām kiyā literally means ‘made the work complete’, but as an idiom it can mean to finish someone off or kill. My poetic ‘finished the job for good’ gestures at that idiomatic finality.
The verse repeats kaam (‘work’) in both lines: the medicine could not do its work, while the heart-sickness completed its work. This contrast is kept in the literal and echoed in the poetic.

C.literal:
All plans went upside down, the medicine did not work at all
It was seen that this sickness of the heart finally finished the job.
C.poetic:
All my schemes were overturned, no remedy worked its part,
In the end, death came from the sickness of the heart.
notes: The couplet hinges on a play on the word 'kaam' (work/action). In the first line, 'kaam kiyā' means 'to be effective' or 'to work'. In the second line, 'kaam tamām kiyā' is a common Urdu idiom meaning 'to finish off' or 'to kill'.
'Bīmāri-e-dil' (sickness of the heart) is the standard ghazal trope where the longing for the beloved is portrayed as a physical ailment that defies medical treatment.
The transition from 'tadbīr' (calculated effort/strategy) to 'davā' (medical cure) shows the progression of the lover's desperation—from trying to manage the situation to seeking a cure.

roman: 'mīr' ke dīn-o-maz.hab ko ab pūchhte kyā ho un ne to
qashqa khīñchā dair meñ baiThā kab kā tark islām kiyā
nuance_note: 'qashqa' = Hindu forehead mark, 'dair' = temple. The conventional 'infidel of love' trope, not a literal conversion. Keep the irony and avoid flattening it into a religious claim.

A.literal:
Why do you ask about Meer's religion and creed now?
He lit his hookah, sat for a while, and long ago renounced Islam.
A.poetic:
Why ask of Meer his faith or creed today?
He lit his hookah, sat a while, and cast his Islam away.
notes: The poet uses his pen name 'Meer' in the maqta (the final couplet), a standard convention of the ghazal.
The 'hookah' acts as a symbol of worldly ease, leisure, or the lifestyle of a 'masti' (intoxicated/carefree) person.

The couplet employs the 'Malamati' (blameworthy) tradition, where the Sufi or the lover adopts the persona of a sinner or an infidel to bypass formal religious structures (shariat) in pursuit of Divine Truth.
There is a sharp, humorous irony in the juxtaposition: the profound spiritual state of apostasy is attributed to the trivial, mundane act of sitting down to smoke a hookah.
The phrase 'tark-e-islām' is used here as a poetic trope for the 'rebel lover' who finds the laws of man and formal religion incompatible with the intoxication of love.

B.literal:
Why do you ask now about Meer's religion and faith?
He plucked his lock of hair, sat in the temple, and long ago abandoned Islam.
B.poetic:
Why seek to know the faith or creed that Meer now holds?
He plucked his lock, sought the temple, and long ago left the fold.
notes: The 'qashqa' (lock of hair) refers to a specific aesthetic of the lover or the dervish; plucking or twisting it symbolizes a break from social norms and an entry into the state of 'Junun' (divine madness).
The 'dair' (temple) is a stock symbol in Urdu poetry representing the realm of the Beloved and the heart's true sanctuary, contrasted with the mosque of formal ritual.

The phrase 'tark-e-islam' (abandoning Islam) is a provocative trope. In the Sufi-influenced ghazal tradition, this rarely means literal conversion, but rather the abandonment of 'Zahir' (outward ritual/orthodoxy) in favor of 'Batin' (the inward path of Love).
The poet uses his takhallus (Meer) to distance himself from the social persona, presenting the 'poet' as a transgressive figure who has found a higher truth in love than in dogma.

C.literal:
Why ask now about Mir's faith and creed? He, after all—
has drawn the qashqa, sat in the temple; long ago he abandoned Islam.
C.poetic:
Ask not now what Mir believes, or by what creed he lives—
He long since drew the qashqa, sat in the temple, renounced Islam.
notes: The sher is signed with the poet's takhallus, 'Mīr,' making the confession a self-dramatizing ghazal gesture.
'dīn-o-mazhab' pairs 'dīn' (faith/religion) and 'mazhab' (creed/school), giving the question an inquisitorial formality.
'qashqa' is a ritual forehead mark, like a tilak, associated with Hindu ascetics; drawing it is a public sign of crossing religious boundaries.
'dair' is the temple/monastery, the ghazal's stock opposite of the mosque and Kaaba; sitting there completes the image of leaving Islam.
'kab kā' is idiomatic for 'long ago,' even though it resembles a question; I translated it as 'long since/long ago.'
The rhetoric is hyperbolic and blame-seeking: the speaker has supposedly abandoned Islam so completely that asking about his faith now is absurd.

roman: ḳhudī ko kar buland itnā ki har taqdīr se pahle
ḳhudā bande se ḳhud pūchhe batā terī razā kyā hai
nuance_note: 'ḳhudī' is Iqbal's technical term for selfhood, not 'ego' or 'pride'. Raise it so high that God asks His servant, before each decree, what is your will?

A.literal:
Exalt your selfhood to such an extent that before every destiny
God Himself asks the servant, 'Tell me, what is your will?'
A.poetic:
Exalt your Self to such heights that before any decree of fate,
God Himself asks His servant, 'Tell me, what is your desire?'
notes: The term 'Khudi' is the cornerstone of Iqbal's philosophy; it is not 'ego' in the pejorative sense, but the realization of the divine spark and the strengthening of the individual's spiritual agency.
The couplet subverts the traditional theological concept of 'Taqdir' (predestination) by suggesting that a perfected human will can become a co-creator with the Divine.
The word 'Banda' (servant/slave) is used to maintain the traditional relationship between Creator and creature, even as the poem describes an unprecedented elevation of that creature.
The use of 'khud' (himself) in the second line emphasizes the intimacy and directness of the Divine encounter.

B.literal:
Elevate your selfhood to such a height that before every destiny,
God Himself asks the servant, 'Tell me, what is your will?'
B.poetic:
Exalt your Self to such a height that before fate is decreed,
God Himself asks His servant: 'Tell Me, what is your will?'
notes: Khudi is the central pillar of Iqbal's philosophy; it is not 'ego' in the pejorative sense, but the realization of the unique, divine spark within the individual.

The couplet presents a paradox regarding 'Taqdir' (predestination). While Islamic theology generally views fate as divine decree, Iqbal suggests that through the perfection of the Self, a human can reach a state where their will aligns with the Divine Will.

The use of 'Banda' (servant) emphasizes the traditional hierarchy, making the act of God asking the servant's preference a powerful reversal of roles, signifying the ultimate empowerment of the human spirit.

C.literal:
Make the self so high that before every destiny
God Himself asks the servant: tell, what is your will?
C.poetic:
Raise the self so high that before each fate is decreed,
God Himself asks His servant: Say, what is your will?
notes: ḳhudī is Iqbal's central term for a strong, creative selfhood; I render it as 'the self' rather than 'ego' to keep its positive moral charge.
taqdīr means destiny as divinely decreed; 'before each fate is decreed' keeps the sense of God's written decree.
razā (will/consent/pleasure) normally appears as God's razā; here God asks the human's razā, an inversion that gives the verse its force. English 'will' cannot fully echo that religious colouring.
The repetition of ḳhud/ḳhudī (self/selfhood and Himself) links human self-realization with God's own direct address; English partly carries it with 'self'/'Himself'.
The couplet does not contain Iqbal's takhallus.

roman: nahīñ hai nā-umīd 'iqbāl' apnī kisht-e-vīrāñ se
zarā nam ho to ye miTTī bahut zarḳhez hai saaqī
nuance_note: Barren field ('kisht-e-vīrāñ') as the poet's people; a little moisture would make the soil fertile. The cupbearer (saaqī) is addressed. Political-revivalist allegory.

A.literal:
Iqbal is not despairing of his barren field;
if it gets a little moisture, then this soil is very fertile, O cup-bearer.
A.poetic:
Iqbal is not hopeless of his field gone bare—
Just wet this earth a little, cup-bearer; it is rich beyond compare.
notes: kisht-e-vīrāñ (barren field) is a stock metaphor for a person, nation, or spiritual state that has become unproductive; Iqbal uses it for the Muslim ummah or the self.
zarḳhez (fertile) is the key contrast: the soil's potential richness is latent, awaiting only 'nam' (moisture).
nam (moisture) carries a double sense: literal water for the field, and wine or spiritual grace (faiz) in the Sufi register—hence the address to the saaqī.

saaqī as addressee is a ghazal convention: the wine-pourer / cup-bearer who can also stand for God, the spiritual guide, or the beloved. Here the moisture and fertility metaphor makes 'saaqī' function as one who waters rather than pours wine.
The pen name 'Iqbal' embedded in line one is the maqt'a convention; the poet speaks about himself in the third person.

B.literal:
Iqbal is not hopeless of his desolate field
If there is a little moisture, this soil is very fertile, O Cupbearer
B.poetic:
Iqbal does not despair for his barren field;
With but a little moisture, this soil is most fertile, O Cupbearer
notes: The poet uses his pen name 'Iqbal', which also means 'prosperity' or 'good fortune', creating a subtle irony: a man named 'Prosperity' is tending to a 'desolate field'.
The 'desolate field' (kisht-e-vīrāñ) is a classic metaphor for the state of the Muslim Ummah or the spiritual condition of the self during a period of decline.
The 'moisture' (nam) is a symbol for divine grace, spiritual inspiration, or the 'water of life' (Ab-e-Hayat) necessary for revival.

The 'Sāqī' (cupbearer) is a traditional Sufi figure who serves the wine of divine love/knowledge; here, the poet addresses the Sāqī to request the 'moisture' of inspiration to revive the parched land.

C.literal:
Iqbal is not hopeless of his desolate field,
If it is slightly moist, this soil is very fertile, O Saaqi.
C.poetic:
Iqbal despairs not of his wasteland's barren state,
A touch of dew, O Saaqi, and this soil shall bloom great.
notes: The pen name 'Iqbal' is a double entendre; while it refers to the poet, the word itself means 'good fortune' or 'prosperity,' suggesting that prosperity is not hopeless even in ruin.
The 'desolate field' (kisht-e-vīrāñ) is a symbol for the decayed state of the community (the Ummah) or the dormant potential of the human soul.
The 'moisture' (nam) is a metaphor for spiritual awakening, divine grace, or the 'wine' of knowledge provided by the Saaqi.
The 'Saaqi' is a stock symbol in the ghazal tradition; here, he represents the spiritual guide or God, the only one capable of providing the 'moisture' needed for rebirth.

roman: ḳhuub parda hai ki chilman se lage baiThe haiñ
saaf chhupte bhī nahīñ sāmne aate bhī nahīñ
nuance_note: 'chilman' = bamboo screen used for purdah. 'ḳhuub parda hai' is ironic: what a veil, neither quite hidden nor coming forward. Playful coquetry.

A.literal:
It is a fine veil that [they] are sitting close to the curtain,
[They] neither hide clearly nor come into view.
A.poetic:
A perfect veil it is, clinging to the screen,
Neither fully hidden, nor clearly to be seen.
notes: The couplet plays on the concept of liminality—the state of being on a threshold. The beloved is neither 'present' (in front of the curtain) nor 'absent' (hidden behind it), but occupies the space of the curtain itself.

There is a subtle distinction between 'parda' (the abstract concept of veiling/modesty) and 'chilman' (the physical object of the curtain). The poet suggests the physical proximity to the curtain has become a 'perfect veil' in itself.

Dagh Dehlvi is known for his 'muhavra' (idiomatic) and 'asl' (natural) style. Unlike the more metaphysical Ghalib, Dagh uses this imagery to describe the teasing, flirtatious ambiguity of the beloved's presence.
The word 'saaf' (clearly/completely) functions as an intensifier, emphasizing that the ambiguity is not accidental but absolute.

B.literal:
Quite a veil it is, that they sit pressed against the screen;
They neither hide completely, nor do they come before me.
B.poetic:
A masterful veil indeed, to cling so close to the screen;
Neither fully hidden, nor revealed to be seen.
notes: The 'chilman' is a specific cultural symbol: a translucent muslin curtain used in traditional households to allow women to see out without being fully seen.
The phrase 'lage baithe hain' (pressed against) suggests a teasing proximity; the beloved is not just behind the curtain, but leaning into it, creating a silhouette.
The word 'saaf' (clearly/completely) creates a paradox: the veil is meant to hide, but because the beloved is so close to the thin fabric, the concealment is incomplete.
Dagh Dehlvi is known for 'muamlaati' poetry—focusing on the flirtatious, worldly dynamics of love rather than the abstract or divine longing found in other Sufi poets.

C.literal:
What a fine veil/screen it is: they sit pressed against the curtain—
plainly they neither hide, nor come forward into view.
C.poetic:
An excellent veil indeed—they sit close to the screen,
plainly neither hidden, nor plainly to be seen.
notes: parda means both a physical veil/curtain and the cultural institution of purdah/seclusion; chilman is a split-bamboo screen, giving the scene a domestic, flirtatious intimacy.

The wit lies in the paradox: sitting close to the curtain creates a tantalizing half-visibility, neither full concealment nor open appearance. The veil is 'excellent' precisely because it leaves the onlooker suspended.
The repeated bhī nahīñ (neither... nor) creates a double negation: not hidden, not manifest. I echoed it with 'neither hidden, nor... seen.'
sāmne ānā idiomatically means 'to come before someone / appear'; I rendered it as 'to be seen' to keep the paradox and rhyme.

roman: urdu hai jis kā naam hamīñ jānte haiñ 'dāġh'
hindostāñ meñ dhuum hamārī zabāñ kī hai
nuance_note: Only we know the language called Urdu; its fame spreads across Hindustan. Pen name 'Dāġh' (literally 'stain/scar') in the final couplet; pride of authorship.

A.literal:
Urdu is the name of the one we know, Dagh,
In Hindustan, the fame of our language is great.
A.poetic:
We know well the one whose name is Urdu, O Dagh,
Across Hindustan, our tongue is the talk of the town.
notes: Dāgh is the poet's takhallus (pen name). While it literally means 'scar' or 'stain', here it serves as the signature of the poet, though it adds a layer of irony—the 'scarred' one claiming the glory of a polished language.

The word 'dhuum' implies more than just fame; it suggests a celebratory noise, a craze, or a blaze of popularity, reflecting Dagh's confidence in the linguistic dominance of Urdu in the Delhi-Lucknow belt.
The emphatic 'hamīñ' (we) asserts a collective identity and pride among the poets and speakers of the era.

B.literal:
Urdu is the one whose name we alone know, Dagh—
in Hindustan there is the din/fame of our language.
B.poetic:
Only we know its name is Urdu, O Dagh—
across Hindustan our tongue's renown rings loud.
notes: The emphatic hamīñ means 'we ourselves/only we,' claiming insider knowledge of the language's true name.
dhuum means both noise and widespread renown; it creates a paradox—everyone in India is talking about the language, yet only the poet's circle truly knows its name.
zabāñ means both 'tongue' and 'language,' so the fame belongs to the spoken word as well as to Urdu itself.
Dāġh is the poet's pen name, used here as a signature and self-address in the ghazal convention; literally it also means 'stain/wound.'
The couplet has a cultural-political edge: in 19th-century India the status and naming of Urdu was contested, and the poet claims proprietary knowledge of it.

C.literal:
We know whose name is Urdu, O Dagh,
In Hindustan, the fame of our language is great.
C.poetic:
We know well its name is Urdu, O Dagh,
In Hindustan, our tongue's renown resounds.
notes: The poet employs his takhallus (pen name), Dāġh, in the maqta (final couplet), a standard convention of the ghazal.
The verse is a 'fakhriyah' (boastful) couplet, where the poet asserts the cultural and linguistic supremacy of Urdu.
The word 'dhuum' is highly idiomatic; it suggests not just fame, but a loud, vibrant, and unmistakable presence—like the sound of a drum or a sudden roar.
Dagh Dehlvi was famous for his command over the 'Zaban-e-Urdu' (the idiom of Urdu), and this couplet serves as a manifesto for the language's vitality and widespread reach.

roman: kitnā hai bad-nasīb 'zafar' dafn ke liye
do gaz zamīn bhī na milī kū-e-yār meñ
nuance_note: Zafar was the last Mughal emperor and died in exile in Rangoon. 'Zafar' means 'victory'. Not even two yards of earth in the beloved's lane (homeland). The attribution of this ghazal is disputed; the reviewer should check.

A.literal:
How unfortunate is Zafar for burial,
Not even two yards of earth was found in the beloved's lane.
A.poetic:
How ill-fated is Zafar, that for his final rest,
Not even two yards of earth in the beloved's lane could he find.
notes: Irony of the Pen Name: The poet uses the takhallus (pen name) 'Zafar', which means 'Victory', creating a bitter, tragic irony as he dies in exile and total defeat.
Metonymy of 'Do Gaz': 'Two yards' is a standard idiomatic reference to a grave in Urdu poetry, emphasizing the minimal space required for a human body.

The Beloved (Kū-e-yār): In the ghazal tradition, the 'beloved' is often a person, but here it functions as a poignant metaphor for Delhi—the poet's lost kingdom and home. To be denied burial in the 'beloved's lane' is to be denied a return to his homeland.
Historical Context: This couplet is deeply elegiac, reflecting the pathos of the last Mughal Emperor dying in exile in Rangoon, far from the soil of India.

B.literal:
How unfortunate is Zafar for burial
not even two yards of land was obtained in the beloved's lane.
B.poetic:
How ill-fated is Zafar, even for burial—
no two yards of earth in the beloved's lane was granted him.
notes: Zafar is the poet's pen name (takhallus) and means 'victory'; the line is bitterly ironic because the last Mughal emperor named Victory is utterly ill-fated.
do gaz zamīn (two gaz/yards of earth) is idiomatic for the smallest plot needed for a grave, emphasizing destitution and exile.
kū-e-yār (the beloved's lane/quarter) is a stock ghazal symbol of nearness to the beloved; historically it also evokes Zafar's beloved Delhi, where he wished to be buried but was denied after 1857.
The beloved can be read on human, political, or Sufi planes—earthly beloved, homeland, or the Divine—so burial in the lane means dying in a state of nearness/union.

C.literal:
How unfortunate is Zafar, for burial
not even two yards of land were found in the street of the beloved
C.poetic:
How wretched is Zafar, that for his final rest
Not two yards of earth were granted in the beloved's lane
notes: Zafar: The poet's takhallus (pen name) means 'Victory.' There is a devastating irony in a man named 'Victory' describing himself as 'bad-nasīb' (unfortunate).

Kū-e-yār: In classical ghazals, the 'street of the beloved' is a place of longing. However, for the exiled Emperor Zafar, this is a political and personal allusion to his homeland (Delhi), from which he was banished to Rangoon.

Do gaz zamīn: This is a cultural idiom referring to the minimum space required for a grave. The tragedy is not just the exile, but the denial of the most basic human right: a burial in one's own soil.
The tone shifts from the traditional romantic longing of the ghazal to a historical lament of loss and displacement.

roman: lagtā nahīñ hai dil mirā ujḌe dayār meñ
kis kī banī hai ālam-e-nā-pā.edār meñ
nuance_note: My heart finds no rest in this ruined land; whose fortune ever held in this impermanent world ('ālam-e-nā-pāedār')? Elegiac tone.

A.literal:
My heart does not feel [at home] in the ruined abode.
Who has ever prospered in the impermanent world?
A.poetic:
My heart finds no rest in this desolate place—
who has ever thrived in this world of fleeting grace?
notes: ujḌe dayār (ruined abode) evokes not just a physical ruin but the desolation of Delhi after 1857 and Zafar's own exile, giving the line a personal and historical resonance.
kis kī banī hai is an idiom meaning 'who has succeeded/prospered', built on ban-nā (to become/be made). The rhetorical question implies no one truly thrives in a transient world.
ālam-e-nā-pā.edār is a Persian izāfat construction: 'world of non-lastingness', a stock Sufi phrase for the fleeting material world.
The first line uses lagtā nahīñ with the sense of 'does not feel attached' rather than 'does not seem', playing on the heart's refusal to bond with a ruined, impermanent realm.

B.literal:
My heart does not settle in this desolate land,
Whose [hope/bond] is established in this transient world?
B.poetic:
My heart finds no repose in this ruined land,
Who could build a home in a world so transient?
notes: The phrase 'lagtā nahīñ' refers to the heart's inability to find peace or a sense of belonging, a common trope in poetry of exile.
'UjḌe dayār' (desolate land) functions as a double entendre: it refers to the physical ruins of the poet's surroundings and the metaphorical ruin of the Mughal Empire and his own life.
'Ālam-e-nā-pā.edār' invokes the Sufi concept of the 'fana' or the ephemeral nature of the material world, suggesting that seeking stability in the earthly realm is a futile endeavor.
The second line uses a rhetorical question to universalize the poet's personal grief, moving from his specific exile to the general human condition of impermanence.

C.literal:
My heart does not find rest in this desolate land,
Who has ever survived in this transient world?
C.poetic:
My heart finds no peace in this ruined land,
For who has ever endured in this fleeting world?
notes: The term 'ujḌe dayār' (desolate land) carries a dual meaning: it refers to the poet's personal state of loneliness and the historical reality of the crumbling Mughal Empire and the ruin of Delhi.
The phrase 'ālam-e-nā-pā.edār' (transient world) is a standard Sufi motif, emphasizing the impermanence of all material existence (fana).
The second line serves as a philosophical 'answer' to the first; the heart's unrest is not an anomaly, but a natural response to the fundamental instability of the universe.
The poet, Bahadur Shah Zafar, uses this universal truth to mask his specific political and personal tragedy, a hallmark of the ghazal tradition.

roman: ham aah bhī karte haiñ to ho jaate haiñ badnām
vo qatl bhī karte haiñ to charchā nahīñ hotā
nuance_note: Double standard: we sigh and are disgraced, they murder and no one talks. Akbar is a satirist, so a political reading is also open.

A.literal:
If I even sigh, I become disgraced.
If she even commits murder, no talk arises.
A.poetic:
A sigh from me, and I am disgraced;
she commits murder, and not a whisper rises.
notes: The whole couplet turns on the parallel use of 'bhī' in both lines: even the lover's smallest act, a sigh, brings disgrace, while even the beloved's greatest act, murder, brings no public censure.
'aah' is a stock ghazal symbol: the lover's involuntary sigh of pain or longing, sometimes also understood as a curse. I translated it simply as 'sigh' to keep the intimate register.
'qatl' here is metaphorical murder: the beloved kills the lover through beauty, indifference, or cruelty, not literal bloodshed.

'badnām' and 'charchā' are both terms of public reputation, but they are not synonyms. 'badnām' means disgraced or ill-famed; 'charchā' means talk, mention, or gossip. The beloved's killing does not even become a topic of conversation.

The pronouns 'ham' and 'vo' are ambiguous. 'ham' can be singular or plural, and 'vo' can be he, she, or they; in the ghazal tradition 'vo' usually points to the beloved or even the Divine. I used 'I' and 'she' to follow the conventional English ghazal idiom.
This couplet does not contain the poet's pen name, so no takhallus appears here.

B.literal:
Even if we sigh, we become infamous,
Even if they murder, there is no talk of it.
B.poetic:
If I but sigh, I am branded with shame,
Yet they may kill, and no one speaks their name.
notes: The couplet relies on a sharp contrast between the 'minimal' act of the lover (a sigh) and the 'maximal' act of the beloved (murder).
The word 'aah' (sigh) is a stock symbol in the ghazal for the lover's silent suffering, but here it is paradoxically treated as a scandalous act.
The term 'qatl' (murder) carries a double meaning: it refers to the literal killing of the lover, but also the metaphorical 'slaughter' of the heart by the beloved's indifference.
The contrast between 'badnām' (infamy) and 'charchā' (public mention) highlights the hypocrisy of social morality where the victim is judged and the oppressor is ignored.

C.literal:
Even when we merely sigh, we become infamous;
Even when they commit murder, there is no talk of it.
C.poetic:
Even a mere sigh of ours brings us disgrace;
Even their murders leave not a single trace.
notes: The couplet relies on a sharp juxtaposition between 'aah' (a sigh, a minor expression of sorrow) and 'qatl' (murder, a capital crime) to highlight social injustice.

The wordplay centers on the disparity of social consequence: the speaker's smallest vulnerability leads to 'badnām' (loss of reputation/infamy), while the beloved's/ruler's greatest crime results in no 'charchā' (public discourse or scandal).

While the 'beloved' (vo) is a standard ghazal trope, Akbar Allahabadi is a master of satire; here, 'they' likely refers to the ruling class or the hypocritical elite, transforming a romantic lament into a biting social critique.
The contrast between being 'branded' by a sigh and 'silenced' by a murder underscores the theme of impunity versus persecution.

roman: huuñ maiñ parvāna magar sham.a to ho raat to ho
jaan dene ko huuñ maujūd koī baat to ho
nuance_note: Moth and candle (parvāna/sham'a): I am the moth, but let there be a candle, let there be night; ready to give my life, if only there were a reason.

A.literal:
I am a moth, but there must be a candle and there must be night.
I am present to give my life, provided there is some reason.
A.poetic:
I am the moth, but let there be a candle, let there be night;
I am ready to die, if there is a cause to make it right.
notes: The 'parvāna' (moth) and 'sham.a' (candle) are the most iconic symbols of the ghazal, representing the lover's desire for total annihilation (fana) in the presence of the Beloved.
Akbar Allahabadi is famous for his wit and satire. Here, he subverts the trope of the 'blind, irrational lover.' Instead of unconditional surrender, he presents a conditional one.

The word 'baat' is the pivot of the couplet. While it usually means 'talk' or 'matter,' here it implies a justification or a worthy cause. He is essentially saying: 'I'll play the part of the tragic lover, but only if the aesthetics are correct and the reason is valid.'

B.literal:
